title: Joint Distributions, Independence and Covariance
summary: Real problems involve several random quantities at once: the two dice, the height and weight of a person, the numbers of successes in two groups of trials. This chapter studies how random variables are related. We define joint and marginal PMFs,…

intro.x: Real problems involve several random quantities at once: the two dice, the height and weight of a person, the numbers of successes in two groups of trials. This chapter studies how random variables are related. We define joint and marginal PMFs, independence of random variables, and the quantities covariance and correlation that measure linear dependence. We then use them to find variances of sums and to analyse classical problems.

blocks.x: For discrete random variables $X,Y$ on the same probability space, the joint PMF is $p_{X,Y}(x,y)=\Prob(X=x,\,Y=y)$.
The joint PMF is non-negative and sums to $1$ over all pairs $(x,y)$. For any set $A\subseteq\R^2$, $\Prob((X,Y)\in A)=\sum_{(x,y)\in A}p_{X,Y}(x,y)$.
$p_X(x)=\sum_yp_{X,Y}(x,y)$ and $p_Y(y)=\sum_xp_{X,Y}(x,y)$.
The events $\{Y=y\}$ partition $\Omega$, so $\{X=x\}=\bigsqcup_y\{X=x,Y=y\}$. Apply countable additivity.

blocks.name: Nuance
blocks.title: marginals do not determine the joint distribution

blocks.x: Many different joint PMFs have the same marginals. For example, let $X,Y$ each be Bernoulli$(1/2)$. Taking $Y=X$ gives joint mass $1/2$ on $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$; taking $Y=1-X$ gives mass $1/2$ on $(0,1)$ and $(1,0)$; taking independent $X,Y$ gives mass $1/4$ on each of the four points. The marginals are identical in all three cases, but the relationships between the variables are completely different.
If $g:\R^2\to\R$ and $\sum_{x,y}\abs{g(x,y)}p_{X,Y}(x,y)<\infty$, then $\Exp[g(X,Y)]=\sum_{x,y}g(x,y)p_{X,Y}(x,y)$.
The proof is the same as for Theorem 4.13: group the pairs $(x,y)$ by the value of $g(x,y)$, and regroup the absolutely convergent series.
Discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ are independent if the events $\{X=x\}$ and $\{Y=y\}$ are independent for all $x,y$:
p_{X,Y}(x,y)=p_X(x)\,p_Y(y)\quad\text{for all }x,y.
Random variables $X_1,\dots,X_n$ are mutually independent if $\Prob(X_1=x_1,\dots,X_n=x_n)=\prod_i\Prob(X_i=x_i)$ for all $x_1,\dots,x_n$.

blocks.name: Proposition
blocks.title: Independence passes to sets and functions

blocks.x: If $X,Y$ are independent discrete random variables then
$\Prob(X\in A,Y\in B)=\Prob(X\in A)\Prob(Y\in B)$ for all sets $A,B$;
$f(X)$ and $g(Y)$ are independent for all functions $f,g$.

(i) Sum the factorisation over $x\in A$, $y\in B$: $\sum_{x\in A}\sum_{y\in B}p_X(x)p_Y(y)=\bigl(\sum_{x\in A}p_X(x)\bigr) \bigl(\sum_{y\in B}p_Y(y)\bigr)$. (ii) Apply (i) with $A=f^{-1}(\{u\})$ and $B=g^{-1}(\{v\})$: $\Prob(f(X)=u,g(Y)=v)=\Prob(f(X)=u)\Prob(g(Y)=v)$.
If $X,Y$ are independent and integrable, then $XY$ is integrable and $\Exp[XY]=\Exp[X]\Exp[Y]$.

By Theorem 6.3 and the factorisation of the joint PMF, $\Exp[XY]=\sum_{x,y}xy\,p_X(x)p_Y(y)=\bigl(\sum_xxp_X(x)\bigr)\bigl(\sum_yyp_Y(y)\bigr)$, the rearrangement being justified by absolute convergence (the same computation with $\abs x\abs y$ shows $\Exp\abs{XY}=\Exp\abs X\Exp\abs Y<\infty$).

blocks.name: Common pitfall
blocks.title: the converse of Theorem 6.6 is false

blocks.x: $\Exp[XY]=\Exp[X]\Exp[Y]$ does not imply independence. Example 6.10 below shows uncorrelated, strongly dependent variables.
For random variables with finite second moments, the covariance is
\Cov(X,Y)=\Exp\bigl[(X-\mu_X)(Y-\mu_Y)\bigr]=\Exp[XY]-\Exp[X]\Exp[Y],

(the two forms agree by expanding the product and using linearity), and, if both variances are positive, the correlation is $\rho(X,Y)=\dfrac{\Cov(X,Y)}{\sigma_X\sigma_Y}$. They are uncorrelated if $\Cov(X,Y)=0$.
$\Cov(X,X)=\Var(X)$ and $\Cov(X,Y)=\Cov(Y,X)$.
$\Cov(aX+b,\,cY+d)=ac\,\Cov(X,Y)$.
Bilinearity: $\Cov\bigl(\sum_ia_iX_i,\sum_jb_jY_j\bigr)=\sum_{i,j}a_ib_j\Cov(X_i,Y_j)$.
$\Var\bigl(\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\bigr)=\sum_i\Var(X_i)+2\sum_{i<j}\Cov(X_i,X_j)$.
If $X,Y$ are independent then $\Cov(X,Y)=0$; hence the variance of a sum of independent variables is the sum of the variances.

(i), (ii) are immediate from the definition. (iii) Expand the product inside the expectation and apply linearity. (iv) By (i) and (iii), $\Var(\sum X_i)=\Cov(\sum_iX_i,\sum_jX_j)=\sum_{i,j}\Cov(X_i,X_j)$; the diagonal terms are the variances and the off-diagonal terms appear twice. (v) By Theorem 6.6.

If $\Exp[X^2],\Exp[Y^2]<\infty$ then $\bigl(\Exp[XY]\bigr)^2\le\Exp[X^2]\Exp[Y^2]$, with equality iff $aX+bY=0$ almost surely for some $(a,b)\ne(0,0)$. Consequently $\abs{\rho(X,Y)}\le1$, and $\abs\rho=1$ iff $Y$ is an exact linear function of $X$.

For every real $t$, $0\le\Exp[(X+tY)^2]=\Exp[X^2]+2t\Exp[XY]+t^2\Exp[Y^2]$. If $\Exp[Y^2]=0$ then $Y=0$ almost surely and the inequality is trivial; otherwise this quadratic in $t$ is non-negative for all $t$, so its discriminant is non-positive: $4(\Exp[XY])^2-4\Exp[X^2]\Exp[Y^2]\le0$. Equality means the quadratic has a double root $t_0$, i.e. $\Exp[(X+t_0Y)^2]=0$ and so $X+t_0Y=0$ a.s. Applying the inequality to $X-\mu_X$ and $Y-\mu_Y$ gives $\Cov(X,Y)^2\le\Var(X)\Var(Y)$, i.e. $\abs\rho\le1$.

Let $X$ be uniform on $\{-1,0,1\}$ and $Y=X^2$. Then $\Exp[X]=0$ and $\Exp[XY]=\Exp[X^3]=0$, so $\Cov(X,Y)=0$. But $Y$ is a function of $X$: for example $\Prob(X=0,Y=0)=1/3\ne\Prob(X=0)\Prob(Y=0)=1/9$.

Correlation zero says that no linear relationship exists; it does not say the variables have no relationship at all. In Example 6.10 the dependence is perfect but non-monotone. For jointly Gaussian variables (Chapter 8) uncorrelated does imply independent; this is a special feature of the Gaussian family.
If $X,Y$ are independent integer-valued random variables, then $Z=X+Y$ has PMF
p_Z(z)=\sum_xp_X(x)\,p_Y(z-x).
The event $\{Z=z\}$ is the disjoint union over $x$ of $\{X=x,Y=z-x\}$; apply independence to each term.
Let $X,Y$ be independent.
If $X\sim\mathrm{Bin}(m,p)$ and $Y\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)$ (same $p$), then $X+Y\sim\mathrm{Bin}(m+n,p)$.
If $X\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda)$ and $Y\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(\mu)$, then $X+Y\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda+\mu)$.
(i) By convolution and Vandermonde’s identity (Theorem 1.16),

\Prob(X+Y=z)=\sum_k\binom mkp^kq^{m-k}\binom n{z-k}p^{z-k}q^{n-z+k}
=p^zq^{m+n-z}\sum_k\binom mk\binom n{z-k}=\binom{m+n}zp^zq^{m+n-z}.
(ii) By convolution and the binomial theorem,
Part (i) matches the story: $X+Y$ counts successes in $m+n$ independent trials. Part (ii) matches the Poisson limit: merging two independent streams of rare events gives a stream with the total rate.

blocks.name: Example
blocks.title: Variance of the binomial via independence

blocks.x: $X\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)$ is a sum of $n$ independent Bernoulli$(p)$ variables, each with variance $pq$. By Theorem 6.8(v), $\Var(X)=npq$, matching Theorem 5.3. Similarly $\mathrm{NB}(r,p)$ is a sum of $r$ independent Geom$(p)$ variables (the waits between successes), so its variance is $r\cdot q/p^2$.
Let $X=\sum_{j=1}^nI_j$ as before, with $p=K/N$ and $q=1-p$. Then $\Var(I_j)=pq$. For $i\ne j$,
\Prob(I_i=I_j=1)=\frac KN\cdot\frac{K-1}{N-1},
so
Using Theorem 6.8(iv):

\Var(X)=npq+n(n-1)\Bigl(-\frac{pq}{N-1}\Bigr)=npq\Bigl[1-\frac{n-1}{N-1}\Bigr]
=npq\,\frac{N-n}{N-1}.
The covariance is negative: drawing a red ball makes red slightly less likely next time. When $N\to\infty$ the covariance vanishes and we recover the binomial.

There are $n$ types of coupon, each new coupon uniformly random and independent. Let $T$ be the number of coupons collected until all $n$ types have appeared. Write $T=T_1+\dots+T_n$ where $T_i$ is the number of additional coupons needed to get the $i$th new type after having $i-1$ types. While we hold $i-1$ types, each draw gives a new type with probability $p_i=(n-i+1)/n$, so $T_i\sim\mathrm{Geom}(p_i)$. By linearity,
\Exp[T]=\sum_{i=1}^n\frac1{p_i}=\sum_{i=1}^n\frac n{n-i+1}=nH_n\approx n(\ln n+\gamma).

The $T_i$ are independent (the number of draws needed at each stage depends only on fresh draws), so $\Var(T)=\sum_i\frac{1-p_i}{p_i^2}=\sum_i\frac{n(i-1)}{(n-i+1)^2}\le\frac{\pi^2}6n^2$. For $n=52$ cards (drawing with replacement) the mean is $52H_{52}\approx236$ draws.

Perform $n$ independent trials, each resulting in category $i\in\{1,\dots,r\}$ with probability $p_i$ ($\sum p_i=1$). Let $X_i$ be the number of trials in category $i$. Counting sequences (Theorem 1.17),

\Prob(X_1=n_1,\dots,X_r=n_r)=\frac{n!}{n_1!\cdots n_r!}p_1^{n_1}\cdots p_r^{n_r},
\qquad n_1+\dots+n_r=n .

Each marginal $X_i$ is $\mathrm{Bin}(n,p_i)$. For $i\ne j$ write $X_i=\sum_t\indic_{\{\text{trial }t\text{ in }i\}}$ and $X_j=\sum_s\indic_{\{\text{trial }s\text{ in }j\}}$. Indicators from different trials are independent, so only $s=t$ contribute to the covariance; in the same trial the indicators cannot both be $1$: $\Cov=\sum_t(0-p_ip_j)=-np_ip_j$. The counts are negatively correlated: a larger count in one category leaves fewer trials for the others.

Variances of counts that are sums of dependent indicators are computed with $\Var(\sum I_j)=\sum\Var(I_j)+\sum_{i\ne j}\Cov(I_i,I_j)$, and $\Cov(I_i,I_j)=\Prob(\text{both})-\Prob(I_i)\Prob(I_j)$. The only new work is the joint probability of pairs. Typical applications: fixed points in a permutation (variance is $1$ for $n\ge2$; check this), records, runs, edges in a random graph.
Two fair dice give $X$ (first) and $M=\max$. Find the joint PMF table, the marginals, and $\Cov(X,M)$.
Prove that if $X,Y$ are independent then $\Var(X-Y)=\Var(X)+\Var(Y)$.
Prove $\Cov(X+Y,X-Y)=\Var(X)-\Var(Y)$.
Show that for a uniformly random permutation of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ the number of fixed points has variance $1$ for $n\ge2$. (Indicators; $\Prob(\text{both fixed})=1/(n(n-1))$.)
Let $X,Y$ be independent Geom$(p)$. Find the PMF of $X+Y$ and recognise it as a negative binomial.
Prove that if $X,Y$ are independent Poisson variables then, conditionally on $X+Y=n$, $X\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,\lambda/(\lambda+\mu))$.

(Collisions) $m$ balls are thrown into $n$ boxes uniformly and independently. Find the expected number of empty boxes and of pairs of balls in the same box. For which $m$ (in terms of $n$) is the expected number of colliding pairs about $1$?
In the coupon collector problem find the exact value of $\Var(T)$ for $n=2$ and verify it using the formula.
(Challenge) Prove that $\abs{\rho(X,Y)}=1$ implies $Y=aX+b$ almost surely, and that the sign of $a$ equals the sign of $\rho$.
